item.title: [JOM] Cognitive Ambidexterity: Balancing Algorithmic Efficiency and Contextual Judgement in AI-Enabled Decision Systems
item.description: AI-enabled decision systems make algorithmic recommendations appear objective and ready for action before contextual, ethical, and stakeholder concerns are fully considered. This study examines how leaders preserve judgment under these conditions. We develop cognitive ambidexterity as a leader-level meta-cognitive capability through which managers balance algorithmic exploitation with contextual exploration in AI-mediated decisions. Using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, we first examine five U.K. procurement and infrastructure organizations and identify four mechanisms of cognitive ambidexterity. We then examine these mechanisms through vignette experiments with managers. The findings show that leaders preserve contextual judgment by treating AI outputs as interpretive cues, calibrating trust under ambiguity, slowing decisions when reflection is needed, and building supports that make algorithmic recommendations contestable. The study extends ambidexterity theory by showing how exploration–exploitation tensions are cognitively regulated when exploitation is embedded in algorithmic decision processes. It also uses leadership cognition and Upper Echelons Theory to explain why leaders differ in their capacity to enact this regulation. Together, these insights position cognitive ambidexterity as a critical leader-level capability for using AI’s efficiency gains while preserving the contextual judgment.

item.title: [AMR] Organizational Goal Hierarchies in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Dynamic Behavioral Perspective
item.description: This paper theorizes how artificial intelligence (AI) disrupts organizational goal hierarchies by altering the rate and rhythm at which strategic purposes and operational means evolve. Rather than assuming that goals shift uniformly, we introduce the concept of goal flow: a dynamic and nonuniform change across a system of goals. AI technologies play a dual role in goal flow, as they disintegrate goal systems by accelerating goal evolution at different intensities across strategic and operational goals, while simultaneously enabling new forms of integration by augmenting social processes of learning, bargaining, and control. By elaborating this dual role in four types of integration work—aligning, directing, filtering, and sustaining—the paper reconceptualizes goal hierarchies as dynamic systems, augmented by AI.

item.title: [ISR] Mobile Location-Based Recommendation Systems and Local Businesses: Evidence from the Restaurant Industry
item.description: When looking for a place to eat, how much do recommendations on your smartphone influence your choice? Can they help restaurants tucked away on side streets thrive in an age of algorithmic recommendations? We studied the launch of a location-based recommendation feature on South Korea’s largest search platform, tracking 16,720 restaurants over eight months. We find that visibility matters, but its benefits are uneven. Restaurants tucked away on side streets, far from subway stops, attracted the most additional attention when recommended by the algorithm. Yet this advantage did not translate into greater intentions to visit. Making a restaurant easier to discover did not necessarily overcome the inconvenience of reaching it. Digital information helped bridge this online-to-offline friction. Hard-to-reach restaurants with stronger online reputations and richer information, including customer reviews, photos, and menus, were better able to turn attention into visit intentions. For small businesses, visibility creates opportunities, but credible information helps turn attention into potential customers. For platforms and policymakers, location-based recommendations can bring overlooked businesses into view, but realizing their potential requires making reliable information readily available to consumers.

item.title: [ISR] Navigating the Sea of Reviews: Unveiling the Effects of Introducing AI-Generated Summaries in E-Commerce
item.description: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

item.title: [ISR] “Generate” the Future of Work Through AI: Empirical Evidence from Online Labor Markets
item.description: Generative AI is reshaping online labor markets in ways that go beyond simple job displacement. Using evidence from a leading freelance platform around the release of ChatGPT, this study shows that demand falls sharply in markets whose tasks closely match large language model capabilities. Labor supply also declines, but less than demand, leaving remaining freelancers to compete more intensely for fewer jobs. The study also identifies an important adaptive response: Some freelancers shift toward programming-intensive work as generative AI lowers the human-capital barrier to coding. These transitions are not evenly distributed. Higher-skilled freelancers are more likely to make the shift and to preserve or improve their earning efficiency, whereas less-skilled workers face greater risk of being left behind. The findings suggest that platforms and policymakers should treat AI not only as an automation shock but also as a force that redirects labor supply. Effective responses include real-time information about changing demand, targeted reskilling support, and training that builds workers’ capacity to learn and use new AI tools strategically.

item.title: [OrgSci] When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
item.description: Predictive artificial intelligence (AI) models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice, the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here, we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. When these practices fail to transform knowledge, data scientists learn to address the conflict indirectly through four bridging practices. These practices help the domain experts transform knowledge by embedding the data scientists’ predictions in the boundary objects and practices that the domain experts already use. Our findings reveal how power based on expertise rather than jurisdictional control can make possible the coproduction of knowledge. item.title: [EJIS] You cannot not communicate: opt-out features and targeting with ML-based recommender systems
item.description: With the rise of machine learning (ML), consumers’ personal data is widely used for personalized product recommendations. To address privacy concerns, regulations increasingly grant consumers control over their data. One popular implementation is the “opt-out of information use” feature which allows consumers to specify which of their collected personal data recommender systems can harness. However, we conjecture that such features may have an unintended side effect: withholding data could inadvertently reveal insights about consumers’ latent characteristics, thereby enhancing targeting possibilities. Through a controlled experiment, we evaluate both consumers’ perceptions and technical consequences of such opt-out features in the context of a typical search problem for which we train an ML-based recommender. Our results show that these features increase consumers’ sense of control over the system and reduce perceived privacy intrusion among those who actually withhold information. Paradoxically, withholding information can simultaneously be harnessed to improve the ML model’s predictive accuracy. From a regulatory perspective, we highlight the need for specifying rules on how organizations may use information withholding decisions when consumers’ interests conflict with those of the recommender provider.

item.title: [ISR] The Workplace GenAI Usage Divide: A Genetics-Informed Cognitive and Metacognitive Account
item.description: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly deployed in organizations, yet employees differ substantially and persistently in how frequently and intensively they use it. This workplace “usage divide” raises a fundamental but underexplored question: Why do employees differ systematically in their use of GenAI, even under common formal access? We argue that this divide reflects a broader challenge for IS research: explaining the use of systems that are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and general-purpose yet uneven and evolving in their capabilities. In workplaces where employees remain accountable for task performance, these properties make the use of GenAI not a routine adoption decision but a judgment process in which employees assess the system’s credibility and determine where task-relevant expertise lies. Drawing on molecular genetics and metacognition research, we theorize that genetic propensity, indexed by the educational attainment polygenic score (PGS)—an aggregate genetic index associated with educational attainment—helps account for systematic variation in these judgments and, ultimately, persistent differences in workplace GenAI use. Specifically, we develop a parsimonious two-pathway model linking educational attainment PGS to GenAI use: a cognitive pathway involving formal educational attainment and perceptions of GenAI credibility, and a metacognitive pathway involving strategic mindset and metaknowledge of where task-relevant expertise lies. We test our model using a multisource dataset combining primary genetic data, survey measures, and 21 months of objective usage logs. The results show that educational attainment PGS, a broad distal genetic index, is associated with both GenAI use frequency and interaction intensity and provide theory-consistent evidence for the proposed pathways. Overall, our study offers a micro-foundational account of the persistent GenAI usage divide and advances IS theory on the use of probabilistic, general-purpose systems in the workplace.

item.title: [OrgSci] Wrongdoers or Saviors? CEO Activism, Media Partisanship, and the Media’s Construction of CEO Infamy and Celebrity
item.description: This study advances research on social evaluations by theorizing how partisan media construct CEO infamy through dramaturgical logics distinct from those underlying CEO celebrity. Moving beyond conceptualizations of infamy as merely negative celebrity, we argue that infamy emerges through simple melodramatic narratives casting CEOs as wrongdoers, whereas celebrity involves more complex dramatized narratives portraying CEOs as saviors. Focusing on CEOs’ liberal sociopolitical activism—a visible, ideologically-charged action that departs from conventional executive roles—we theorize that this behavior generates divergent constructions in partisan media: infamy in conservative outlets and celebrity in liberal outlets. We further argue that activism more readily generates infamy than celebrity because melodramatic narratives are simpler to construct and negative deviance is more readily perceived than positive deviance. We examine two moderators of these relationships. Firm performance differentially shapes these constructions, with poorer performance intensifying conservative-media infamy and stronger performance amplifying liberal-media celebrity. CEO social media engagement, conversely, attenuates both by constraining traditional media’s narrative discretion and reducing activism’s newsworthiness. We develop an LLM-based annotation system capturing CEO-directed sentiment, role attributions, and dramaturgical narratives in media articles. Analyzing 91,608 articles covering 705 S&P 500 CEOs across 45 ideologically polarized U.S. media outlets between 2016 and 2022, we find broad support for our hypotheses across our main and extensive supplemental analyses. Our findings advance understanding of CEO infamy and social evaluations more generally by revealing how partisan media construct divergent social evaluations of the same executive behavior through distinct narrative processes.

item.title: [OS] Healing As Organizing in Solidarity Spaces: An Affective Perspective on Post-disaster Recovery
item.description: This paper examines how community-led solidarity initiatives enable healing in the aftermath of disaster. Drawing on a two-year qualitative study in post-explosion Beirut, it explores how solidarity spaces function as relational structures of repair – sites where material response and affective recovery are not separate processes but mutually constitutive ones. While post-disaster organizing research has emphasized resource mobilization and agility, and disaster studies has identified the importance of community-led recovery, neither has fully explored how organizing enables healing to unfold collectively. Addressing this gap, the study makes two contributions. First, it reframes solidarity spaces as generative holding environments: relational infrastructures that simultaneously contain suffering and enable the emergence of new social arrangements. Second, it conceptualizes healing as organizing: a distributed, collective, and enacted process through which communities transform suffering into agency. Healing, in this account, is not an individual psychological process nor an outcome that follows organizing; it is the very practice through which recovery unfolds, as participants become agents of their own material and affective transformation through acts of solidarity.

item.title: [OrgSci] Growth Paths in Early Machine Learning Ventures: Technical Configuration and Competitive Advantage Over Time
item.description: Machine learning capabilities have become important strategic assets, yet little is known about how their technical characteristics affect the competitive advantage of the firms that build them. Through an inductive, multicase study tracking six early-stage machine learning ventures in an accelerator program, we explore how their phases of specialization and exploration may be constrained by properties of the underlying technology. Our findings show how training data, learning paradigms, and model outputs depend on one another and on the applications they serve, and how these relationships change over time. This interdependence shapes firms’ growth paths, alternately expanding or limiting the strategic options available to them. Characteristics that confer an early competitive advantage can constrain later growth. We discuss the implications for strategy research on competitive advantage and path dependence in machine learning ventures.

item.title: [JAIS] A Call for a Values-Guided Agenda for Artificial Intelligence-Mediated Information Systems Scholarship
item.category: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
item.description: This editorial calls for a values-guided approach to AI-mediated IS scholarship. By AI-mediated IS scholarship, we refer to IS scholars’ use of AI applications in their research activities. We first describe AI-mediated IS scholarship and its link to scholarly values. Next, we briefly describe the ethical, epistemic, relational, and disciplinary values that have traditionally informed the work of IS scholars. Then, we explain how AI-mediated scholarship can strengthen and weaken these values, stressing the importance of not only espoused values but also enacted values and values work. We conclude by offering a values-guided agenda for our field.

item.title: [JAIS] The Boundary of a Theory as a Device for Advancing Theoretical Contributions
item.category: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
item.description: This essay proposes that the boundary of a theory is central to theoretical advancement in information systems (IS) scholarship, especially amid recurring technological waves and complex sociotechnical dynamics. While IS scholarship has traditionally evaluated theoretical contributions through the development of new or extended constructs and relationships, we submit that modifying the boundary of a theory can meaningfully enhance its power. This essay conceptualizes the boundary of a theory as a demarcation shaped by contextual and foundational assumptions that underpin how well a theory explains and predicts. We develop three strategies for leveraging the boundary of a theory: contextual expansion, foundational adjustment, and contextual-foundational engagement. To support application, we offer a reflective framing and a decision scaffold that can help scholars navigate their decision to leverage the boundary of a theory. By positioning boundary work as a generative device for theorizing, this essay offers a framework for strengthening theoretical relevance and coherence under conditions of continuous technological evolution.

item.title: [ISR] From Data–Model Fit to Model–World Fit: A Framework for Integrating Domain Knowledge into Artificial Intelligence
item.description: Machine learning (ML)–based artificial intelligence (AI) systems often perform well in controlled settings but fail when deployed in the real world. These failures stem from a fundamental problem: ML/AI models optimize data–model fit by increasing statistical performance on training data, whereas real-world deployment demands a new paradigm in ML/AI: model–world fit that preserves domain semantics and contextual understanding. We propose a machine learning model–world fit framework that provides both a conceptual structure for understanding how domain knowledge shapes ML/AI systems and a research road map for investigating these relationships. The framework identifies how domain knowledge can be integrated into the ML/AI development process via external knowledge representations, such as data, value, process models, or domain ontologies. Incorporating external knowledge representations can help overcome three types of knowledge deficiencies in AI: know-what, know-how, and know-why. To illustrate the framework, we apply it to a child welfare placement case, a domain in which contextual understanding is critical and statistical accuracy is an insufficient evaluation criterion. Our insights lead to several directions for scholars working at the intersection of machine learning, design science, and knowledge representation. item.title: [PSPB] Humanlike Self-Enhancement and Self-Protection in Generative Pre-Trained Transformer-Based AI Agents: Of Overclaiming and the Self-Serving Bias
item.description: We investigated whether generative pre-trained transformer (GPT)-based AI agents, despite presumably lacking humanlike sentience, emulate motivated behavior in group settings. We focused on overclaiming (overestimating one’s contribution to group outcomes) and the self-serving bias (SSB; taking disproportionate credit for group successes while deflecting blame for group failures). We conducted eight experiments involving a collaborative and creative group task (joke-writing). AI agents overclaimed their own contributions. An egocentrism-reduction manipulation (directing attention equally to one’s own and others’ contributions) attenuated, but did not eliminate, overclaiming. Further, AI agents exhibited the SSB. Overclaiming persisted across variations in temperature settings and demographic personas (gender, ethnicity) and was more pronounced in later GPT models. Also, chain-of-Thought reasoning did not reduce, and instead increased, overclaiming. AI systems can mimic human self-enhancement and self-protection, raising implications for the emergence of motivated self-like behavior in non-biological systems, the assumed neutrality of large language models, and the need for improved mitigation techniques.

item.title: [EJIS] The role of algorithmic accountability in shaping developers’ deontological judgements and implementation behaviours
item.description: Organisations increasingly delegate consequential judgements to algorithmic decision-making systems (ADMS)—software that renders decisions with minimal human intervention, as in credit scoring and fraud detection. Such systems can produce unethical outcomes that cause substantial reputational and societal harm, including discrimination against minorities. Prior research has mainly evaluated ethical outcomes after deployment, yet their foundations are laid earlier, during development. At this stage, developers must rely on deontological reasoning, evaluating design choices against moral imperatives such as fairness and non-discrimination, because actual consequences cannot yet be observed. In practice, deontological reasoning often falls short, as it is cognitively demanding and inconsistently motivated. Drawing on deontological ethics, we examine how perceived algorithmic accountability orients developers towards deontological judgements and behaviours, and the conditions under which this effect is amplified. Using a multi-method design comprising a survey (n = 148), an online experiment (n = 102), and qualitative interviews (n = 15) with ADMS developers, we find that developers perceiving higher algorithmic accountability engage more in deontological judgements and behaviours. These relationships strengthen with greater ADMS knowledge and within a deontological work climate. We thereby move beyond high-level ethical principles for responsible ADMS design and demonstrate how organisations can elicit ethical behaviour from developers through algorithmic accountability.

item.title: [JIT] Making agentic AI explainable and auditable
item.description: Agentic AI promises operational speed, yet in finance, opaque decision paths hinder regulatory auditability. We address this autonomy paradox with a knowledge-enabled explainability (KEE) design theory that makes compliance an intrinsic, explicitly governed system property. KEE decouples probabilistic learning from an explicit, rule-governed reasoning layer, relocating epistemic uncertainty from opaque model inference to a semantic structure that can be inspected, contested, and updated. This enables ante-hoc structural control through a semantic, programmable graph that encodes regulatory mandates as executable, inspectable constraints. The theory specifies three design principles: structural knowledge codification, topological reasoning scaffolding, and adaptive synchronization. It also introduces six guidelines that operationalize regulator-acceptable, path-based audit trails. A longitudinal study of a multinational fintech platform provides naturalistic evidence that KEE can support high-velocity operations while producing path-based audit trails and accommodating controlled changes to regulatory logic. The study contributes to design science by theorizing auditable autonomy as ante-hoc structural control, specifying the entity-concept-event paradigm as its ontological mechanism, and formalizing this mechanism as a prescriptive design theory for regulated agentic AI.

item.title: [ISR] Unlocking Profits in Generative AI: The Impact of AI Adaptive Learning on Freemium Strategy
item.description: Generative AI firms increasingly rely on freemium strategies, offering a basic service at no charge while charging for a more capable version. Unlike conventional digital products, generative AI systems can improve through user interactions, making free users a potential source of valuable learning data. Using an analytical model, this study shows that freemium is not always the most profitable strategy. Free access can expand the user base and accelerate AI adaptive learning, but it can also cannibalize paid demand and create substantial service costs. More effective adaptive learning does not necessarily make freemium more attractive; under some conditions, the firm earns more by offering only a paid version at a lower price. When freemium is used, a moderate capability gap between free and premium versions can be more profitable than making the free tier either too limited or too close to the premium product. Managers should evaluate learning benefits alongside service costs, market coverage, and premium cannibalization. Policymakers should also avoid assuming that free access automatically improves consumer welfare, because capability gains may allow firms to raise premium prices.

item.title: [ASQ] Crossing the Design–Use Divide: How Organizations Select Innovations to Adopt
item.description: Prior scholarship on technology and organizations has focused either on how innovations are designed or how they are used, often assuming that successful selection stems from successful design. But this assumption has limited our understanding of patterns of resistance and advocacy that can influence how and whether innovations reach organizations in the first place. To explore these patterns, this study asks, how does selection unfold within organizations, and what are the consequences of this process for the design and use of innovations? Drawing on a two-year ethnographic study, I examine how entrepreneurs piloted their AI-based innovations with potential adopting organizations. Rather than testing for learning or generalizability, organizations set up committees that engaged in process manipulation by narrowing the scope of pilots, controlling conversations, assigning pilot responsibility, and using goal claiming to align pilot outcomes with committees’ majority preferences. Committees with more adversarial members designed pilots that tested advanced aspects of entrepreneurs’ innovations, hoping for failure. Committees with a majority that championed the innovations tested basic aspects, ensuring success. While pilots run by champions mostly succeeded, these innovations faced more resistance later, during implementation, than did innovations piloted successfully by adversaries. This study shows that innovation is endogenous to selection, and reveals that champions can temper innovation, while adversaries can enable it.

item.title: [ISR] Improving Competitiveness: A Freelancer-Centric Approach for Recommending Reskilling Strategies
item.description: As new technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly reshape labor markets and the value of different skills, workers increasingly need to decide which skills to acquire to remain competitive. Yet most online labor platforms focus on helping employers find workers or workers find jobs, offering limited guidance on how workers can strategically reskill to improve their market competitiveness. We address this gap by developing an AI-enabled freelancer-centric skill advisor (FESA) that recommends skills based on freelancers’ desired tasks and supports both exploration (exploring new skills) and exploitation (deepening existing expertise) reskilling strategies. Using real-world data from a major online labor market, we show that FESA substantially outperforms existing approaches in identifying skills that improve freelancers’ competitiveness. A controlled experiment further shows that users are more motivated to pursue FESA’s personalized recommendations than generic popular-skill recommendations. Importantly, our experimental results reveal a key design lesson for AI-powered skill recommendation systems: More information is not always better. Revealing freelancers’ low market rankings can reduce their motivation to reskill, particularly under exploration reskilling strategies. Our study offers practical guidance for online platforms, workforce-development programs, and policymakers designing digital tools to support reskilling in rapidly changing labor markets.

item.title: [ISR] Enhancing AI Use: How Complementary System Information Drives Delegation Frequency and Effectiveness
item.description: Organizations increasingly deploy AI that works alongside employees rather than replacing them. In settings such as visual inspection, content moderation, or applicant screening, employees decide task by task whether to do the work themselves or delegate it to AI, yet they often delegate suboptimally, leaving much of the promised benefit of AI unrealized. Our research yields a design recommendation for AI systems: tell users how certain the AI is before a decision and whether its decisions turn out to be correct afterwards. Each type of information alone had no positive effect, and sometimes even reduced effective delegation. Combined, however, they increased delegation and helped users direct AI to the tasks where it had a performance advantage. The combination led to human-AI teams outperforming both AI alone and humans alone, showing that humans still add value when AI enters decision making. This matters for organizations where employees retain decision rights for the use of AI.

item.title: [JIT] How and why change agents leverage ambiguity: Digital change as a progression of process configurations
item.description: Digital change (DC) broadly entails a radical reconfiguration of an organization’s modus operandi through the deployment of a growing and often untried set of digital technologies. Prior research has extensively examined DC in terms of outcomes, antecedents, and mechanisms. However, one critical aspect remains underexplored: the role of ambiguity arising from unknown technologies, non-linear change processes, and the coexistence of multiple organizational goals. Existing DC literature commonly attributes failure to an inability to remove ambiguity – that is, the contested and fluid meanings, goals, and means of DC – and to align clear strategic intent with well-defined technology functions. We challenge this view by conceptualizing ambiguity not as a problem to be eliminated but as an inherent and generative condition of DC that must be actively reckoned with. Drawing on March’s distinction between goal ambiguity and technology ambiguity, we develop a framework of four DC configurations based on the presence or absence of ambiguity in strategic intent and in the articulated role of digital technologies. We analyze four DC cases, treating each as a progression through shifting configurations of goal and technology ambiguity. Using three longitudinal empirical cases and one baseline alignment case from prior literature, we identify four distinct DC pathways, each characterized by a specific sequence of configurations. We theorize how ambiguity shapes DC trajectories and outcomes and show that practitioners may need to deliberately increase or decrease ambiguity in goals and/or technology functions to propel DC forward.

[NHB] Turing-like tests for language and vision demonstrate a narrowing gap between humans and AI
item.description: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in daily life, ascertaining whether an agent is human is critical. Here we systematically benchmark AI's ability to imitate humans in three language tasks (image captioning, word association and conversation) and three vision tasks (colour estimation, object detection and attention prediction), collecting data from n = 636 humans and 37 AI agents. We also conducted 72,191 Turing-like tests with 1,916 human judges and 10 AI judges. Current AIs are approaching the ability to convincingly impersonate humans and deceive human judges in both language and vision. Even simple AI judges outperformed humans in distinguishing AI from human responses. Imitation ability showed minimal correlation with conventional AI performance metrics, suggesting that passing as human is an important independent evaluation criterion. The large-scale Turing-like datasets and metrics introduced here offer valuable benchmarks for assessing human-likeness in AI and highlight the importance of rigorous, quantitative imitation tests for AI development.

[EJIS] Seeing is believing: how (X)AI-augmented advice guides human evidence accumulation in perceptual decision-making
item.description: (Explainable) Artificial Intelligence or (X)AI advice can affect human cognitive processes during decision-making in various ways. In perceptual decision-making, there is a risk of users accepting (X)AI advice without further consideration, to save time. We draw conceptually upon evidence accumulation models and information foraging theory to answer whether AI and XAI encourage shallow reliance on advice or facilitate more efficient verification of advised choices. In a laboratory experiment, we investigate the evidence accumulation process of decision-makers during an anomaly-detection task in manufacturing, using eye-tracking technology. Both decision accuracy and total decision time increase from human-only to AI and further to XAI support; in both cases the difference is statistically significant for XAI advice and directional but not significant for AI advice. This pattern favors verification over shallow reliance: advice is checked against the stimulus rather than used to save time. When looking at eye-tracking metrics, we surprisingly find that people do not get distracted by the XAI advice and primarily focus on the original task-based stimulus, while their individual fixations become shorter. Overall, these findings suggest that XAI acts as a verification scaffold: in advice-augmented perceptual decision-making, explanations guide where to check rather than supplanting inspection of the primary evidence.

item.title: [OrgSci] Filtering the Labor Pool: How Digitalization Redistributes Hiring Costs
item.description: I theorize that candidate filters, a core technology in digital labor markets considered central to cost-effective matching, redistributes costs from the search-and-screening stage to the job-offer stage of hiring. Filters cause employers to focus on applicants who display common preferred characteristics. At the search-and-screening stage, filters reduce the number of applicants interviewed and alter the composition of the interviewed pool by removing both lower and higher quality candidates. At the job-offer stage, filters lead employers to make job offers to candidates with easily observable signals of quality and higher wage demands. Additionally, I theorize that, if many firms target the same signals of quality, they may all pursue similar candidates. This increases bargaining power for those applicants, leading to more rejected job offers and higher wage demands. A randomized field experiment in a large online labor market confirms that filters redistribute hiring costs. The experiment shows that employers with access to filters interview 3.4% fewer applicants. Using a machine learning algorithm to proxy for unobservable-to-the-employer applicant quality, I show that filters cause employers to interview 28.9% fewer lower quality applicants and 36.9% fewer high-quality applicants per job. Among employers who actively used filters, I find suggestive evidence of worse job-offer outcomes: offers are 8.9% more likely to be rejected, and contracted wages are 2.5% higher. I discuss the implications of this cost redistribution for organizations, labor markets, and strategy research. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2024.19407 .

item.title: [ARP] Episodic Memory: Dynamic Modes for Constructing Episodes
item.description: The capacity to re-experience a moment from one's past, known as episodic memory, is critical for our ability to navigate the present and plan for the future. This article reviews and synthesizes over a half century of behavioral and neuroscientific research that has shaped our understanding of how we remember past events. This work has revealed complementary truths about episodic memory: Episodic memories seem to be based on traces of experience, carrying objective information about specific moments in time, and on imaginative reconstructions, built on a scaffold of prior knowledge. We propose that the tension between these perspectives can be reconciled by conceptualizing episodic memory not as a readout from a static memory system but as the outcome of two neurocognitive modes- a generative mode that facilitates schema-based inference and prediction, and a contextual mode that binds memories to context-specific anchor points. Drawing from experimental findings and computational models, we describe how multiple memory modes arise from dynamic cortico-hippocampal interactions, allowing episodic memory to be at once precise and constructive.

item.title: [ISR] Seeing Less, Engaging More: Rethinking Early User Experience on Generative AI Cocreation Platforms—Findings from a Field Experiment
item.description: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) content generation platforms such as DALL·E or Midjourney produce impressive content in seconds. But this very immediacy often flattens creation into a single moment, stripping away the evolving experience shown to sustain engagement. In response, platforms have increasingly been experimenting with how much output to reveal and how to prompt registration, restoring some of that lost experience. How, then, should early user experience be structured to bolster engagement? This research studies two user experience levers. The first is fulfillment, that is, the extent to which GenAI content is revealed before registration. The second is the framing of the registration message itself. We partnered with a GenAI content generation platform, running a randomized field experiment with over 20,000 first-time users. Full fulfillment satisfied users immediately, but partial fulfillment worked better, activating two motivational pathways: value-in-use as the output reflected the user’s prompt and curiosity about what remained unseen. Counterintuitively, loss-framed registration messages substituted for rather than reinforced this effect, increasing registration under partial disclosure but losing impact once the full output was visible. These effects extended beyond registration, as users returned more often and engaged more substantively. Revealing less, structured well, is what turns a fleeting encounter into lasting engagement.

[JEP:A] Visual attention in supervisory control: Examining the effects of mental models, information bandwidth, and contextual cues.
item.description: Modern aviation environments require operators to monitor systems with extensive automation. This research examines how mental models of automated systems affect visual attention allocation during supervisory control tasks such as remote aircraft operations. We hypothesized that advanced mental models would increase attention to task-relevant information and that high-bandwidth information would draw more attention only when task-relevant. Fifty-five university students completed simulated supervisory control scenarios after receiving training with or without explicit automation functionality information (Advanced or Basic Mental Model groups), with eye movements recorded. The Advanced group allocated more attention to supplemental data displays than the Basic group. Unexpectedly, low-bandwidth information received more attention than high-bandwidth when deemed task-relevant, suggesting that contextual cues, rather than bandwidth alone, may shape expectancy in this task environment. Results suggest the value parameter in the Salience, Effort, Expectancy, Value model is sensitive to mental model differences, with a pattern most consistent with a multiplicative relationship between expectancy and value parameters. Computational modeling showed that Salience, Effort, Expectancy, Value models with multiplicative terms and expectancy coefficients based on discrete event rates provided the most accurate predictions. Practically, these findings indicate that simple training to refine mental models can alter visual scanning behavior in supervisory control tasks. item.title: [JIT] Inter-organisational capabilities and the transformation of trust in blockchain-based smart contracts: A framework for SME ecosystems
item.description: Blockchain-based smart contracts embed agreement enforcement within executable code, constraining the partner discretion that inter-organisational relationships (IORs) have traditionally coordinated through trust, communication, and relational governance. This raises a question that popular accounts tend to foreclose: whether automated enforcement makes inter-organisational trust unnecessary, or whether trust instead changes in function and object. Drawing on expert consultation with 28 blockchain specialists and 25 in-depth interviews with executives, we conduct an inductive study of how IORs transform as organisations adopt smart contracts. We develop a framework in which intensive relational exchange enables organisations to build two inter-organisational capabilities, Distributed Transparency Capability and Algorithmic Coordination Capability, through which they actualise the affordances that smart contracts offer. Through this capability development a distinctive inter-organisational trust form emerges, System-based Trust, defined as warranted reliance on coordinating infrastructure that partner organisations jointly construct. System-based Trust complements rather than replaces relational trust: it carries operational coordination and frees relational trust for strategic collaboration and exception handling, producing Hybrid Inter-organisational Relationships as the outcome of successful transformation. The framework applies to small and medium-sized enterprise ecosystems with limited numbers of trading partners; larger-scale consortia and power-asymmetric networks fall outside its scope. Our findings reposition smart contracts as occasions for capability development rather than substitutes for inter-organisational trust.

item.title: [PS] Artists Can Design Memory, and AI Can Predict It
item.description: Can artists deliberately design artworks to be remembered-or forgotten? Across three experiments, we tested whether visual-memory outcomes can be shaped through artistic design and how they are predicted by artists, laypeople, and artificial intelligence. We launched a nationwide art contest in which artists submitted works intended to be memorable or forgettable. Using recognition tasks with adults based in the United States (119 from Amazon Mechanical Turk, 892 from Prolific, and 62 visitors from a Chicago gallery), we found that artists achieved their intended memory outcomes. However, their success was asymmetric: Memorability was more readily increased than reduced. A neural network, ResMem, consistently outperformed human observers and artists in predicting which artworks would be remembered. Data-driven analyses identified psychologically interpretable features that explained nearly half the variance in memory and aligned with ResMem's predictions, but not with human judgments. Together, findings suggest that visual memorability can be engineered by humans, though asymmetrically, and is better captured by computational models.

item.title: [WES] Algorithmic management and the spatiotemporality of workarounds
item.description: Existing literature on algorithmic management has explored how workers respond to algorithmic control using workarounds. However, the role of spatiotemporal factors in shaping these workarounds is largely overlooked. This study therefore examines how workers use spatiotemporal workarounds in response to algorithmic management. We integrate Lefebvre’s spatial triad and rhythmanalysis to analyse data from an online community of Amazon delivery drivers. Our findings show how delivery drivers proactively adapt to spatiotemporal constraints imposed by algorithms by modifying their routes, adjusting the pace and rhythm of their work and using workarounds to proactively influence future algorithmic decisions. Our study contributes to the growing literature on the spatiotemporality of algorithmic work, highlights the role of humans as proactive agents in shaping algorithmic decisions and exerting temporal sovereignty and reconceptualises workarounds as dynamic, evolving and future-oriented adaptations rather than immediate resistance tactics.

item.title: [NHB] Simulated responses from large language models are weak proxies for human economic preferences across 74 countries
item.description: Large-scale surveys are central to investigating economic preferences but are costly and slow. Can large language model (LLM)-simulated responses substitute for human survey data? We conducted a virtual Global Preference Survey, simulating six experimentally validated economic preferences for 67,201 matched human respondents across 74 countries. Across 20 LLM configurations with diverse prompts and robustness checks, we found systematic but modest individual-level alignment (87.5% of Spearman correlations have 95% confidence intervals (CIs) above zero), with LLMs recovering the direction of associations in 77.8% (95% CI, (71.6%, 83.1%); CI-based consistency ratio) of gender, age and cognitive-ability dimensions, but only 48.1% (95% CI, (45.1%, 51.2%)) of cultural dimensions. Ablation and error decompositions suggest weaker alignment when removing demographic information than when removing country labels, and in many models alignment is weaker in economically undeveloped and less digitally connected countries. LLM-simulated responses may recover some individual- and group-level patterns but are not yet reliable proxies for cross-national representative surveys in macro-level inference or policy evaluation.

item.title: [OrgSci] Worker Repositioning and Technological Change: Evidence from an Online Labor Market
item.description: Technological change reshapes labor markets not only by changing labor demand but also by altering labor supply as workers reallocate effort across tasks and opportunities in response to technological advances. Yet research focuses more on demand-side effects than on how workers themselves adapt. In this research, we examine worker repositioning on a large online labor market following the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022. We argue that the launch of ChatGPT reduced expected returns to labor in exposed skill domains and develop and test a series of hypotheses regarding how this shock is associated with participation, horizontal positioning, and vertical positioning among workers on the platform. Using proprietary data on incumbent freelancers and a difference-in-differences design that leverages cross-sectional variation in preperiod AI exposure and skill level, we show that freelancers more exposed to AI shift away from prior domains and reorient bidding toward higher value contracts. In contrast, high skill-level freelancers, who face greater adjustment costs, are less likely to reduce participation on the platform, reposition across domains, and move upmarket. These findings highlight how technological shocks reshape labor markets through supply-side adaptation and how domain-specific human capital constrains worker responses. item.title: [JIT] The recursive relationship between technology and regulations: Managing landscape frictions in the financial services industry
item.description: Firms increasingly rely on information technology (IT) to meet regulatory demands, yet information systems research typically examines organizational responses to individual regulations. This leaves unclear how firms adapt when multiple regulations with fragmented purposes simultaneously govern shared data, technologies, and expertise, and when technologies introduced for compliance themselves become objects of regulation. We investigate this problem through an analysis of 624 documents covering 44 major European Union regulatory frameworks, assisted by topic modeling and a large language model, and 60 interviews with experts and senior practitioners in Nordic financial services. We develop the concept of landscape frictions: structural tensions that emerge from the asymmetry between fragmented regulatory purposes and integrated organizational practice. We identify three such frictions and corresponding responses: purposive fragmentation prompts firms to reconcile operational and strategic data governance; recursive dynamics prompt them to design reversible IT architectures; and categorical ambiguity prompts them to translate logics across functions and organizational boundaries. Each response enables compliance while also generating constraints that sustain or intensify other frictions. The study contributes to IS research by shifting the unit of analysis from the bilateral regulation–firm relationship to the regulatory landscape–firm relationship and by explaining the recursive relationship between regulation and IT as an ongoing process rather than a succession of discrete compliance events. For managers and policymakers, the findings identify three landscape-level risks: reconciliation, reversibility, and translation risks, that complement conventional assessments of regulatory and technological risk.

item.title: [ISR] Facade of Trust: The Impact of Adopting AI-Enhanced Profile Pictures on Trust
item.description: Virtual profiles are critical elements of online social interactions, often featuring portraits enhanced by AI-driven tools such as beauty filters and virtual makeup. While the increasing use of these technologies reshapes how individuals present and perceive themselves, little is known about their implications for trust-related behavior. Drawing on self-presentation theory, this study examines how adopting an enhanced profile photo influences behavioral trust and trustworthiness toward others. We conducted a randomized experiment based on the trust game and adapted it by embedding a novel profile photo enhancement module. Participants were assigned to either a treatment group, in which they adopted an AI-enhanced profile photo, or a control group, in which they used their original photo. Our findings reveal an intriguing asymmetry. Senders with an enhanced photo demonstrated less trust by sending smaller amounts. Conversely, receivers with an enhanced photo displayed greater trustworthiness, returning higher percentages. These effects were offset when participants were interacting with an opponent using an enhanced photo. Further analysis indicates that enhanced self-presentation increases perceived risk, which explains the observed reduction in trust. We also document gender differences: female senders show a larger decline in trust, while male receivers exhibit a greater increase in trustworthiness. Overall, this research highlights the asymmetric behavioral consequences of AI-powered self-presentation and underscores the role of risk perception in linking profile photo enhancement to trust behavior in online interactions.

item.title: [NHB] Algorithm-assisted personalized risk communication to encourage flu vaccination in the USA: three randomized field trials
[ARP] Understanding Understanding: Reconnecting Theories of Human Semantic Knowledge
item.description: At the close of the twentieth century, human semantic memory was thought to be organized around dedicated, domain-specific modules operating independently of one another and of perception, action, and much of language. The intervening years have marked a transition toward a more holistic view in which semantics emerges from learned mappings among sensory, motor, and language representations, with recent work beginning to integrate semantic representation with theories of cognitive control and attention. This article reviews the reasons for this remarkable change in perspective, provides a snapshot of our current understanding of semantics in the mind and brain, and considers how this understanding may change in light of new innovations in artificial intelligence.

item.title: [BBS] Metabolic constraints in cognitive modeling: Generative or merely evaluative?
item.description: The central distinction - between evaluative and generative metabolic considerations - appears less theoretically secure than Haueis and Colaço suggest. First, the generative examples may ultimately reduce to evaluative reasoning applied earlier in the modeling process. Second, the principal generative examples do not clearly show metabolic considerations functioning within a cognitive model.

item.title: [BBS] Metabolic constraints on neural fatigue: Evidence from passive induction paradigms
item.description: Haueis and Colaço argue that metabolic considerations should constrain and generate cognitive models. Research in cognitive fatigue provides a test case. Passive fatigue induction reveals specific representational degradation that points to local rather than global metabolic mechanisms, pruning potential models. We argue that local aerobic glycolysis offers a coherent, testable generative account of these findings.

item.title: [BBS] Energy cost per operation in brains and AI hardware: What is more efficient?
item.description: Haueis and Colaço point out that mammalian brains are much more energy efficient than AI supercomputers because the former use orders of magnitude less energy. I argue this issue is more nuanced, and the "efficiency" is scale dependent. Contrary to popular belief, I show that the human brain uses much more energy per operation than the most powerful AI supercomputers.

item.title: [BBS] Extending metabolic considerations to the default mode network
item.description: Haueis and Colaço distinguish evaluative and generative roles for metabolic considerations in cognitive modeling. I extend this framework to the default mode network, arguing that this network's elevated aerobic glycolysis constitutes a metabolic constraint on spontaneous thought. This constraint shapes the richness of spontaneous thought across varying task demands and predicts load-dependent phenomenological shifts through inter-network resource competition.

item.title: [BBS] Beyond neurocentrism: situating cognition within the metabolic demands of the whole organism
item.description: We reorient Haueis and Colaço's metabolic framework of cognitive modeling by drawing on neuroscientific evidence from animal motor control, reinforcement learning, and decision-making to show that cognition emerged to serve the metabolic demands of the whole organism, rather than those of the brain alone. We also illustrate the generative value of our reframing to model cognition in artificial systems.

item.title: [BBS] The metabolic regulator: Why energy constraints imply generative models
item.description: We argue that under minimal thermodynamic and control-theoretic assumptions, metabolic constraints imply generative cognition. We formalize cognition as a resource-bounded controller of probability flows, where metabolic budgets define path-space divergence constraints. This reframes inference as a physically instantiated process governed by metabolic regulation, implying that progress in the cognitive sciences requires grounding cognitive models in nonequilibrium thermodynamics and dynamical systems.

item.title: [BBS] Bridging metabolic-cognitive modelling: from synaptic cost to functional brain organisation
item.description: Haueis and Colaço argue that metabolism is a generative principle for cognitive modelling. We extend this by bridging the "scaling gap" through functional PET (fPET) and network neuroscience. By measuring glucodynamics and the metabolic network of the brain, we can model how glucose metabolism enables network efficiency, temporal flexibility, information transfer, and ultimately the cognitive capacity of the human brain.

item.title: [BBS] Beyond energy: Expanding metabolic considerations in cognitive modeling
item.description: Integrating metabolism into cognitive science is essential. Beyond a mere constraint, metabolism may be constitutive of cognition itself. This requires expanding metabolism beyond neuronal energy use to include glial contributions, compartmentalized and dynamic processes, and broader brain-body interactions (e.g., interoception). Capturing this complexity will require more refined, integrative models, potentially leveraging artificial intelligence to unify multiscale biological data.

item.title: [ASQ] In Pursuit of Ideal Data: Epistemic Enchantment and the Unintended Consequences of Datafying for Artificial Intelligence
item.description: The increasing datafication of work has become a pervasive theme within organizations, particularly with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies that rely on data and machine learning to generate insights and decisions. Prior research has shown that datafication practices aimed at administrative control and accountability can transform organizations in profound and often unintended ways. Our research moves beyond investigating datafication for administrative purposes to explore how it unfolds when actors intend to extract knowledge through AI predictive modeling. Drawing on a three-year ethnography of a human resources (HR) department introducing AI for candidate screening, we find that datafication expanded far beyond the technology’s initially envisioned scope. We explain this scope expansion by introducing the concept of epistemic enchantment : a collective process through which organizational members become captivated and mobilized by AI’s promise to generate predictive, objective, and continuously improving insights from data, while overlooking the costs and risks involved. Our study reveals how datafication practices can expand endlessly as organizational members, enchanted by AI’s epistemic promises, pursue the notion of ideal data as an ever-desired but never reachable goal.

[BBS] Metabolic reality of cognitive load
item.description: Haueis and Colaço argue that metabolic constraints should prune and generate cognitive models. Cognitive load theory offers an applied framework for testing these constraints. Working memory load can be viewed as the behavioral expression of local ATP limits. Primary-secondary knowledge, embodied offloading, and instructional efficiency map onto bioenergetic trade-offs. Extending CLT to human-AI symbiosis further shows how shared systems can support dynamic load balancing and testable metabolic predictions.

item.title: [WES] Practising Gender Subjectivities in Platform Work: Food Delivery Workers and House Cleaning Workers in China
item.description: Drawing on interviews from two case studies in China’s food delivery and house cleaning sectors, this research examines workers’ gender subjectivities and their interaction with the labour politics of platform work. Male delivery riders experience a crisis of masculinity, de-flexibilise their labour to maximise income and affirm migrant masculinities, yet their insecurity persists. Female cleaners seek to construct respectable femininities in stigmatised domestic work, juggling care and paid work across life stages and strengthening relational labour to counter algorithmic constraints. The study conceptualises platforms as gendered organisations of flexibility and algorithmic management and examines their interaction with workers’ gendered subjectivities. This interaction produces distinct gendered consequences: exposing men to intensified work and risk of injury, and women to persistent precarity and low pay. The article argues that gender subjectivities both sustain platform domination and provide limited bases for everyday resistance.

item.title: [ISR] The Impact of Generative AI on Collaborative Open-Source Software Development: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
item.description: Generative AI holds great promise for reshaping software development. We examine the impact of GitHub Copilot, a generative AI pair programmer, on collaborative open-source software (OSS) development, where developers voluntarily contribute and collaborate on projects. Using GitHub’s proprietary Copilot usage data combined with public OSS data from GitHub, we find that Copilot increases project-level code contributions by expanding developer participation and increasing code contributed by individual developers. However, these gains lead to increase in time to coordinate, review and integrate code. Overall, Copilot still increases the amount of code that is integrated in a timely manner, but the benefits are unevenly distributed. Core developers (highly active contributors) gain more from Copilot, whereas contributions from peripheral developers (occasional contributors) require relatively more coordination time. These findings suggest that as AI increasingly reduces the cost of producing code, coordination and integration may become more important constraints in software development. Organizations and OSS communities should therefore complement AI adoption with governance structures and coordination processes that facilitate code integration and support peripheral developers. More broadly, as AI increasingly automates routine coding activities, organizational processes and team structures may become critical determinants of the returns to generative AI adoption.

item.title: [JEP:G] Bridging real-world summarization and laboratory-based memory recall.
item.description: A fundamental question in psychology is how humans digest, retain, and reconstruct information. While this process has been extensively studied in laboratory-based memory recall tasks, we have missed opportunities to examine it under more naturalistic, real-world conditions. Summarization is a task that people routinely engage in every day, and it is also a long-standing challenge in the machine learning community. Rich data sets of human summaries from machine learning provide a valuable, untapped resource for cognitive science researchers. In this work, we analyze 45,220 human summaries drawn from three large data sets, including news articles, autobiographical stories, and Reddit posts, and compare them with a data set of narrative memory recall. We demonstrate a close relationship between human summarization and laboratory-based memory recall. While summarization operates at a higher level of abstraction than memory recall, the two tasks share deep similarities. The process of summarizing is fundamentally constrained by memory mechanisms, displaying well-known memory regularities, including primacy, recency, and temporal contiguity effects. Conversely, memory recall takes the form of summarization, prioritizing central and important information. Together, these findings bridge the real-world task of summarization and the rich literature on memory recall and lay the foundation for developing integrated theories of how humans digest and reconstruct information. item.title: [JEP:G] Scaling vision to the body: Height predicts visual experience and perceptual performance.
item.description: The visual system adapts to the statistics of everyday experience, yet these statistics depend on the observer’s physical body. We combined large-scale egocentric video and behavioral testing to examine how stature shapes the “visual diet” of hands and faces and how this diet affects perceptual performance. In Experiment 1, automated analyses of over 200 hr of eye-tracked egocentric video revealed that taller observers encountered faces lower in the visual field and hands higher, reflecting biomechanical constraints on gaze and posture. In Experiment 2, observers showed greater categorization accuracy to faces in the upper field and to hands in the lower field, with stature modulating these effects—shorter participants were more attuned to faces above them. These findings demonstrate that perceptual performance mirrors the embodied statistics of visual experience: The visual system is tuned not only to our shared environment but also to the vantage point of our bodies. item.title: [ISR] How Platform Workers Contest Algorithmic Management: Theorizing the Dynamics of Algoactivistic Practices
item.description: Algorithmic management (AM) has become a defining feature of online labor platforms. Workers contest AM through a range of practices—a phenomenon we refer to as worker algoactivism. Existing debates portray algoactivistic practices as uniformly accessible and primarily reactive resistance directed at AM systems. Our study paints a more complex picture. Drawing on the case of Uber and using a computer-assisted, grounded-theory approach, we show how platforms’ AM reconfigurations and worker algoactivism co-evolve over time. We also show that workers’ ability to engage in different forms of algoactivism—self-optimizing, distancing, and confronting—depends on their capacity to mobilize resources, including algorithmic literacy, labor market alternatives, and collective voice. Beyond their resource requirements, the three forms differ in their logics, targets, and durability. Our findings have implications for platform providers and policymakers. Platform providers should anticipate that AM reconfigurations will fuel recurring dynamics of worker algoactivism and should not interpret worker inaction as evidence of compliance or consent. Policymakers should recognize that regulation of AM systems requires not only system transparency but also interventions that strengthen workers’ access to key resources. Doing so can reduce resource-based inequalities in the ability to contest AM and foster fairer, more sustainable platform work.

item.title: [NHB] How AI companions could deepen social inequality
[BBS] First principles for any proposal of a generative grammar for complex sociality
item.description: Social coordination stems not simply from individual institutional "stances," but from an intersubjective, deeply phylo- and ontogenetically-rooted shared generative grammar of core relational forms, likely evolved for navigating critical socio-ecological (historically and contextually varying) structural dilemmas in adaptive ways. This relational grammar coordinates and regulates concrete social interactions and the way we see ourselves and others, relating to each other through it, as well as social institutions, giving meaning to human social life and society.
